Inverse kinematics on guiding vector fields, explained

The paper (Zhou, Bautista, Yao, García de Marina), written out step by step for the paper’s own circle of 100 m and its fixed-wing drone: from the error signal of a path, to an error that obeys a linear system, to the heading rate the aircraft commands, and back to the flight logs

Published

November 14, 2026

From the Swarm Systems Lab, University of Granada. To try the results by hand, open the playground.

What this page does. It takes the paper Inverse Kinematics on Guiding Vector Fields for Robot Path Following (ICRA 2025, arXiv:2502.17313 v1) and writes it out for the paper’s own example: a circle of radius 100 m, flown by a fixed-wing drone at about 15 m/s. It goes step by step: the error signal of a path and the classic guiding field (Section II of the paper), the inverse-kinematics field that makes the error obey a linear system (Lemma 1 and Theorem 1), the oscillation added on purpose around the path (Section III-B), the field for an aircraft that cannot change its speed (Section IV), and the heading law that tracks it (Theorem 2). It ends with the program the aircraft runs, and with the paper’s three flights, simulated again and compared with their logs.

Source and status. The results are the paper’s, and this page does not re-prove them. It adds four things, each marked where it appears: a comparison with the classic field when the path changes size (Section 3), a three-dimensional example (Section 3.2), a check of the formulas after Theorem 2 against the exact derivative, which finds where they differ (Section 7), and a reading of the flight logs of the paper’s repository (Section 10). Equation, figure and remark numbers are those of arXiv v1, the ICRA version. Where this page departs from it because arXiv v1 is not correct, Section 7.1 says so. Every number on the page is computed by core.py when the page is rendered. The interactive figures run assets/core.js, and make check proves that the two agree.

1 The problem

A small fixed-wing drone flies at a constant height. Its horizontal position is p=(px,py)p = (p_x, p_y) and its course is θ\theta. It cannot stop or slow down: its speed vv is fixed by the airspeed (and changed by the wind). The only command is the turn rate ω\omega. This is the paper’s model (10):

ṗ=v(cos⁡θsin⁡θ),θ̇=ω. \dot p = v \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \dot\theta = \omega .

What it measures. Its own position and ground velocity (GPS), so also vv and θ\theta. Nothing else. There is one aircraft and no communication.

The path. A closed curve given by an implicit equation ϕ(p)=0\phi(p) = 0. The paper’s flights use a circle of radius r=100r = 100 m around a centre cc, normalised so that ϕ\phi has no units:

ϕ(p)=∥p−c∥2r2−1. \phi(p) = \frac{\|p - c\|^2}{r^2} - 1 .

So ϕ=0\phi = 0 on the circle, ϕ<0\phi < 0 inside and ϕ>0\phi > 0 outside. The number ϕ(p)\phi(p) is the error signal: it is what the aircraft drives to zero. It is not a distance. With ρ=∥p−c∥\rho = \|p - c\|, ϕ=ρ2/r2−1\phi = \rho^2/r^2 - 1, and a radial error of ρ−r\rho - r metres reads ϕ≈2(ρ−r)/r\phi \approx 2(\rho - r)/r. The paper’s Section V gives the exact conversion, ρ−r=rϕ+1−r\rho - r = r\sqrt{\phi + 1} - r: ϕ=0.1\phi = 0.1 is 4.88 m outside and ϕ=−0.1\phi = -0.1 is 5.13 m inside.

The task. Follow the path, and choose how the aircraft gets there: how fast the error decays, and what it does around the path. The paper’s motivation is concrete. The drone’s dipole antenna radiates badly in some directions, and the bank angle of a long turn can keep it pointed the wrong way for a while. A small, controlled oscillation around the path changes the bank angle all the time. Shaking the roll directly would leave the path; the paper puts the oscillation into ϕ\phi instead, where it has a meaning in metres and stays inside a closed loop.

Why it is hard. Classic guiding fields make ϕ\phi go to zero, but how fast depends on the gradient of ϕ\phi, so on the path, its scale and its normalisation. And an aircraft at constant speed cannot obey a field whose length changes.

2 Step 1: the error signal and the classic field

2.1 What ϕ\phi tells the robot

For a robot in the plane (m=2m = 2, the paper writes the general case p∈ℝmp \in \mathbb{R}^m with m−1m - 1 functions ϕi\phi_i), the chain rule gives the paper’s (1):

ϕ̇=Jϕ(p)ṗ,Jϕ=∇ϕ⊤. \dot\phi = J_\phi(p)\,\dot p, \qquad J_\phi = \nabla\phi^\top .

For the circle, with d=p−cd = p - c,

∇ϕ(p)=2r2d,Hϕ=2r2I2. \nabla\phi(p) = \frac{2}{r^2}\, d, \qquad H_\phi = \frac{2}{r^2} I_2 .

(arXiv v1 prints Jϕ=1r2[2(px−x0),(py−y0)]J_\phi = \tfrac{1}{r^2}[\,2(p_x - x_0),\ (p_y - y_0)\,] in Section V; the second entry misses its factor 2, Section 7.1.) On the path ∥∇ϕ∥=2/r\|\nabla\phi\| = 2/r = 0.020 per metre. Moving along the level set does not change ϕ\phi: the velocities with JϕvT=0J_\phi v_T = 0 are the multiples of E∇ϕE\nabla\phi, with E=(0−110)E = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right) the rotation by 90°90°. That is the paper’s tangent space Tp(ℳϕz)T_p(\mathcal{M}_{\phi_z}), of dimension one. The paper needs ∇ϕ≠0\nabla\phi \neq 0 near the path (Assumption 2). For the circle it fails only at the centre.

2.2 The classic field

The paper’s Example 1 is the classic guiding vector field,

f(p)=vT−Jϕ⊤ϕ=sE∇ϕ−kϕ∇ϕ,s=±1, f(p) = v_T - J_\phi^\top \phi = s\,E\nabla\phi - k\,\phi\,\nabla\phi, \qquad s = \pm 1 ,

(Remark 1, with a gain kk; ss chooses the direction of travel). A robot that follows it exactly has ϕ̇=−k∥∇ϕ∥2ϕ\dot\phi = -k\,\|\nabla\phi\|^2\,\phi. That converges, by the Lyapunov function V=ϕ2/2V = \phi^2/2 of Example 1, but the rate is k∥∇ϕ∥2k\|\nabla\phi\|^2, and it changes with the place, the path and the way ϕ\phi is written.

On the paper’s circle, ∥∇ϕ∥2=4ρ2/r4\|\nabla\phi\|^2 = 4\rho^2/r^4. On the path it is 4.0e-04 per square metre. So with k=1k = 1 the error decays at 4.0e-04 per second, a time constant of 2500 s. Fly a circle of 400 m with the same kk and the rate falls 16 times. The gain of the classic field must be retuned for every path.

Singular points. Where f=0f = 0 the robot stops; where the field is normalised, its direction is undefined. The paper calls this set Ψ\Psi (4) and shows that a guiding field needs JϕJ_\phi of full rank near the path (Proposition 1). For the circle the classic field vanishes only at the centre.

3 Step 2: inverse kinematics on the error

3.1 The field

The paper asks for more than convergence: it wants ϕ̇=uϕ\dot\phi = u_\phi for an input uϕu_\phi it designs (Problem 1). Split the field in two, f=vT+vCf = v_T + v_C, with vTv_T along the level set. Then ϕ̇=JϕvC\dot\phi = J_\phi v_C, and the paper picks vCv_C by inverse kinematics, the least-norm solution of JϕvC=uϕJ_\phi v_C = u_\phi (the paper’s (7) and (8)):

vC=Jϕ⊤(JϕJϕ⊤)−1uϕ=m=2∇ϕ∥∇ϕ∥2uϕ. v_C = J_\phi^\top\left(J_\phi J_\phi^\top\right)^{-1} u_\phi \;\overset{m = 2}{=}\; \frac{\nabla\phi}{\|\nabla\phi\|^2}\, u_\phi .

This is what a robot arm does with its end effector, applied to the error of a path: the Jacobian’s pseudo-inverse turns a desired rate of the error into a velocity.

Lemma 1. vTv_T and vCv_C are orthogonal (vT⊤vC=(JϕvT)⊤(⋅)=0v_T^\top v_C = (J_\phi v_T)^\top(\cdot) = 0), so f≠0f \ne 0 wherever vT≠0v_T \ne 0: no singular points where ∇ϕ≠0\nabla\phi \neq 0.

Theorem 1. ϕ̇=JϕJϕ⊤(JϕJϕ⊤)−1uϕ=uϕ\dot\phi = J_\phi J_\phi^\top (J_\phi J_\phi^\top)^{-1} u_\phi = u_\phi wherever JϕJ_\phi has full rank. With uϕ=−kϕu_\phi = -k\phi the error decays as ϕ(t)=ϕ(0)e−kt\phi(t) = \phi(0)e^{-kt}, whatever the path and its normalisation.

On the circle, vC=−kϕr22ρ2dv_C = -k\,\phi\,\frac{r^2}{2\rho^2}\,d, a radial velocity of −k(ρ2−r2)/(2ρ)-k(\rho^2 - r^2)/(2\rho) m/s. It does not depend on how ϕ\phi is normalised: multiply ϕ\phi by any constant and vCv_C is the same.

What this page adds: the size of the path. Single integrators, both fields with the same tangential speed of 10 m/s, from 1.6r1.6\,r, the classic gain set once to k=2500k = 2500 (a good value for r=100r = 100 m), the IK gain k=0.25k = 0.25. The measured decay rates of |ϕ||\phi|:

radius of the circle IK-GVF, k=0.25k = 0.25 classic field, k=2500k = 2500
25 m 0.237 18.325
100 m 0.249 1.169
400 m 0.250 0.073

The IK-GVF decays at its kk at every size; the classic field’s rate follows k∥∇ϕ∥2∝1/r2k\|\nabla\phi\|^2 \propto 1/r^2. (An aircraft flying the classic field normalised to its speed vv sees the rate vk∥∇ϕ∥v k\|\nabla\phi\| near the path, so ∝1/r\propto 1/r: the playground’s approach race.) Try other paths and starts below.

3.2 In three dimensions

The paper states Theorem 1 for any dimension mm. What this page adds: one example with m=3m = 3. A closed path shaped like the rim of a saddle is the intersection of two surfaces, the cylinder x2+y2=r2x^2 + y^2 = r^2 and the saddle z=h(x2−y2)/r2z = h(x^2 - y^2)/r^2, with r=50r = 50 m and h=20h = 20 m:

ϕ1=x2+y2r2−1,ϕ2=1r(z−hx2−y2r2). \phi_1 = \frac{x^2 + y^2}{r^2} - 1, \qquad \phi_2 = \frac{1}{r}\left(z - h\,\frac{x^2 - y^2}{r^2}\right).

JϕJ_\phi is now 2×32 \times 3. The tangent vTv_T is along ∇ϕ1×∇ϕ2\nabla\phi_1 \times \nabla\phi_2, and vC=Jϕ⊤(JϕJϕ⊤)−1uϕv_C = J_\phi^\top (J_\phi J_\phi^\top)^{-1}u_\phi with uϕ=(−k1ϕ1,−k2ϕ2)u_\phi = (-k_1\phi_1, -k_2\phi_2). Each error then decays at its own rate. With k1=0.3k_1 = 0.3 and k2=0.8k_2 = 0.8 the simulation measures 0.295 and 0.795. The robot first reaches the saddle surface, then slides along it to the cylinder. The playground has this example, and a path where Assumption 2 fails.

The flat end of |ϕ2||\phi_2| near 10−510^{-5} is the 1 ms Euler tick of the simulation, not the field.

4 Step 3: a behaviour around the path

The paper’s Section III-B adds a time signal γ(t)\gamma(t) and a third part vBv_B, chosen so that

Jϕ(vC+vB)=γ̇−k(ϕ−γ)(the paper’s (9)). J_\phi\,(v_C + v_B) = \dot\gamma - k\,(\phi - \gamma) \qquad \text{(the paper's (9))} .

Then ddt(ϕ−γ)=−k(ϕ−γ)\frac{d}{dt}(\phi - \gamma) = -k(\phi - \gamma): the error converges to γ\gamma, exponentially, at the rate kk. With vC=−βkϕv_C = -\beta k\phi the paper’s choice is vB=β(γ̇+kγ)v_B = \beta(\dot\gamma + k\gamma), with β=Jϕ⊤(JϕJϕ⊤)−1=∇ϕ/∥∇ϕ∥2\beta = J_\phi^\top(J_\phi J_\phi^\top)^{-1} = \nabla\phi/\|\nabla\phi\|^2. Both terms of vBv_B are needed. The term βγ̇\beta\dot\gamma alone gives ϕ̇=−kϕ+γ̇\dot\phi = -k\phi + \dot\gamma, whose steady state is γ\gamma filtered by s/(s+k)s/(s + k): smaller, and ahead in phase.

For the paper’s second flight, γ(t)=Asin⁡(wt)\gamma(t) = A\sin(wt) with A=0.1A = 0.1 and w=0.55w = 0.55 rad/s (an 11.4 s period). On the circle that is a radial swing of 4.88 m outwards and 5.13 m inwards. Feeding forward only γ̇\dot\gamma would give an amplitude of 0.091 and a lead of 24.4°.

5 Step 4: an aircraft that cannot slow down

5.1 The field at constant speed

The aircraft flies at the speed vv whatever it does, so the field it follows must have the length vv. The paper’s template (11) keeps ϑ=vC+vB\vartheta = v_C + v_B, which sets ϕ̇\dot\phi, and fills the rest with the tangent:

f=αv̂T+ϑ,v̂T=vT∥vT∥,α=v2−∥ϑ∥2. f = \alpha\,\hat v_T + \vartheta, \qquad \hat v_T = \frac{v_T}{\|v_T\|}, \qquad \alpha = \sqrt{v^2 - \|\vartheta\|^2} .

Because v̂T⟂ϑ\hat v_T \perp \vartheta (Lemma 1), ∥f∥=v\|f\| = v. This works only where ∥ϑ∥≤v\|\vartheta\| \le v, the set Ωb\Omega_b. Outside it the paper flies straight along ϑ\vartheta (its (12)):

f={vϑ/∥ϑ∥,∥ϑ∥>v,αv̂T+ϑ,∥ϑ∥≤v. f = \begin{cases} v\,\vartheta/\|\vartheta\|, & \|\vartheta\| > v, \\ \alpha\,\hat v_T + \vartheta, & \|\vartheta\| \le v . \end{cases}

The two pieces agree on the boundary, where α=0\alpha = 0, so ff is continuous. Its units are metres per second (Remark 3): ϑ\vartheta is the velocity that sets the error, and α\alpha the speed left for travelling along the path.

Ωb\Omega_b on the paper’s circle. Without γ\gamma, ∥ϑ∥=k|ρ2−r2|/(2ρ)\|\vartheta\| = k|\rho^2 - r^2|/(2\rho), so Ωb\Omega_b is the annulus ρ2−r2≤2vρ/k\rho^2 - r^2 \le 2v\rho/k on both sides. For v=15v = 15 m/s and k=0.25k = 0.25 it runs from ρ\rho = 56.6 m to 176.6 m. Inside it, and with the heading aligned with ff, the error obeys ϕ̇=−kϕ\dot\phi = -k\phi exactly (Theorem 1). Outside it the aircraft flies straight towards the path, along ∇ϕ\nabla\phi, and enters Ωb\Omega_b in finite time. With a γ\gamma, ϑ\vartheta changes with time and so does Ωb\Omega_b; with wind, vv changes with the heading and so does Ωb\Omega_b.

6 Step 5: the heading law

The aircraft must turn so that its velocity ṗ\dot p lines up with ff. Both have the length vv. Theorem 2 commands

ω=θ̇c+kθf⊤Eṗv2,θ̇c=f⊤E⊤ḟv2. \omega = \dot\theta_c + k_\theta\,\frac{f^\top E\,\dot p}{v^2}, \qquad \dot\theta_c = \frac{f^\top E^\top \dot f}{v^2} .

θ̇c\dot\theta_c is the rate at which ff turns as seen by the moving aircraft (feed-forward), and f⊤Eṗ/v2f^\top E\dot p/v^2 is the sine of the angle from ṗ\dot p to ff (feedback). With φ=ṗ−f\varphi = \dot p - f and V=∥φ∥2/2V = \|\varphi\|^2/2, the paper finds V̇=−kθ(f⊤Eṗ)2/v2≤0\dot V = -k_\theta(f^\top E\dot p)^2/v^2 \le 0. The aircraft aligns unless it starts flying exactly against the field, and Theorem 1 then holds along the flight.

The derivative of ff. The law needs ḟ\dot f along the motion. This page computes it exactly (the paper’s expressions after Theorem 2 differ, Section 7). With β=∇ϕ/∥∇ϕ∥2\beta = \nabla\phi/\|\nabla\phi\|^2, w=γ̇−k(ϕ−γ)w = \dot\gamma - k(\phi - \gamma) and ϑ=βw\vartheta = \beta w:

β̇=Hϕṗ∥∇ϕ∥2−2∇ϕ(∇ϕ⊤Hϕṗ)∥∇ϕ∥4,ẇ=γ̈−k(∇ϕ⊤ṗ−γ̇),ϑ̇=β̇w+βẇ, \dot\beta = \frac{H_\phi\dot p}{\|\nabla\phi\|^2} - \frac{2\,\nabla\phi\,(\nabla\phi^\top H_\phi \dot p)}{\|\nabla\phi\|^4}, \qquad \dot w = \ddot\gamma - k\,(\nabla\phi^\top\dot p - \dot\gamma), \qquad \dot\vartheta = \dot\beta\,w + \beta\,\dot w ,

and, writing ddtx∥x∥=1∥x∥(I−xx⊤∥x∥2)ẋ\frac{d}{dt}\frac{x}{\|x\|} = \frac{1}{\|x\|}\left(I - \frac{x x^\top}{\|x\|^2}\right)\dot x,

ḟ={v∥ϑ∥(I−ϑ̂ϑ̂⊤)ϑ̇,∥ϑ∥>v,α̇v̂T+α∥vT∥(I−v̂Tv̂T⊤)v̇T+ϑ̇,α̇=−ϑ⊤ϑ̇α,∥ϑ∥≤v, \dot f = \begin{cases} \dfrac{v}{\|\vartheta\|}\left(I - \hat\vartheta\hat\vartheta^\top\right)\dot\vartheta, & \|\vartheta\| > v, \\[2mm] \dot\alpha\,\hat v_T + \dfrac{\alpha}{\|v_T\|}\left(I - \hat v_T\hat v_T^\top\right)\dot v_T + \dot\vartheta, \quad \dot\alpha = -\dfrac{\vartheta^\top\dot\vartheta}{\alpha}, & \|\vartheta\| \le v , \end{cases}

with v̇T=sEHϕṗ\dot v_T = s\,E H_\phi \dot p. Note α̇\dot\alpha: it divides by α\alpha, which is zero on the boundary of Ωb\Omega_b. Section 7 measures what that does.

The figure below is the whole system, from any start, with the paper’s gains of the first flight (k=0.25k = 0.25, kθ=0.6k_\theta = 0.6) and its logged start: 323 m from the centre, heading 149°. The aircraft flies clockwise (s=−1s = -1), as in the flights.

7 Corrections to the published version

The checks of this page, run against arXiv v1, found five things. None of them changes the paper’s main results (Lemma 1, Theorem 1, the flights). Section 7.1 sums up where this page departs from arXiv v1 because of them.

1. The heading rate is unbounded at the edge of Ωb\Omega_b. The paper’s Remark 2 asks for a field smooth enough that the heading rate needed to track it is bounded. Field (12) is continuous, but α=v2−∥ϑ∥2\alpha = \sqrt{v^2 - \|\vartheta\|^2} has an infinite slope where ∥ϑ∥=v\|\vartheta\| = v, and α̇=−ϑ⊤ϑ̇/α\dot\alpha = -\vartheta^\top\dot\vartheta/\alpha appears in θ̇c\dot\theta_c. An aircraft that enters Ωb\Omega_b along ϑ\vartheta sees α\alpha grow like τ\sqrt\tau, τ\tau the time since it entered, so θ̇c\dot\theta_c grows like 1/τ1/\sqrt\tau. Flight 1 again, with a time step of 0.5 ms (it enters at tbt_b = 7.99 s):

time after entering Ωb\Omega_b θ̇c\dot\theta_c (rad/s) θ̇cτ\dot\theta_c\sqrt{\tau}
0.001 s 4.588 0.145
0.01 s 2.072 0.207
0.1 s 0.783 0.248
1 s 0.218 0.218

The product θ̇cτ\dot\theta_c\sqrt\tau stays between about 0.15 and 0.25 while θ̇c\dot\theta_c changes twentyfold: an integrable singularity of the type 1/τ1/\sqrt\tau. The field turns by a finite angle, 27° in the first second, but no aircraft can follow its first instants. In the log of flight 1 the commanded ω\omega jumps from about 0 to 0.71 rad/s at the first sample inside Ωb\Omega_b (the spike of the paper’s Fig. 3), and in the next five seconds the bank angle reaches 31°, against about 12° on the circle. A C1C^1 blend between the two pieces of (12) would remove the spike; that is a design change, not a typo.

2. The expressions for ḟ\dot f after Theorem 2. Taken literally, they differ from the exact derivative in two places. (a) The text says that, outside Ωb\Omega_b, the term v(I∥ϑ∥−ϑϑ⊤∥ϑ∥3)ϑ̇v\left(\frac{I}{\|\vartheta\|} - \frac{\vartheta\vartheta^\top}{\|\vartheta\|^3}\right)\dot\vartheta vanishes because ϑ̇\dot\vartheta is parallel to ϑ\vartheta. That holds only while ∇ϕ\nabla\phi keeps its direction, for example on a circle flown exactly along the radius. In general ∇ϕ\nabla\phi turns as the aircraft moves, and so does ϑ\vartheta. (b) β̇\dot\beta mixes ṗ\dot p and ff, which agree only once the aircraft is aligned. The turn rate of the field, θ̇c\dot\theta_c, at a few states (gains of flight 2, γ\gamma of flight 2 at t=1t = 1 s):

path and state in Ωb\Omega_b θ̇c\dot\theta_c, exact θ̇c\dot\theta_c, as printed
circle yes -0.3042 -0.2984
circle, outside Ωb\Omega_b no 0.0269 0.0000
ellipse no -0.4479 0.0000
rounded square yes -0.5037 -0.4868

Outside Ωb\Omega_b the printed expressions give a field that does not turn at all. The feedback term of the law absorbs the difference: the aircraft is a little less aligned during the approach (about 1° more heading error), and once in Ωb\Omega_b the two versions fly the same. The largest |ϕ−γ||\phi - \gamma| after 40 s, flying the second flight’s γ\gamma from the start of flight 1, on four paths [numerical]:

path ḟ\dot f exact ḟ\dot f as printed
circle 0.0021 0.0020
ellipse 0.0041 0.0042
rounded square 0.0043 0.0041
peanut 0.0083 0.0082

So the printed expressions cost nothing measurable in these flights, but they are not the derivative of ff; this page uses the exact ones (Step 5). The paper’s code (the repository’s gvf_ik.py) writes its own derivatives, and its derivative of a unit vector has sign slips; this page does not reproduce it.

3. The sign of γ\gamma, and the hand-adjusted phase of Fig. 4. The paper drives ϕ→γ\phi \to \gamma (9). The code of the paper’s repository drives e=ϕ+γe = \phi + \gamma to zero, so ϕ→−γ\phi \to -\gamma, and the flight log agrees: its GVF:error column is ϕ+γ\phi + \gamma, so the log holds the γ\gamma that was flown. Fitting sines of w=0.55w = 0.55 rad/s to the 100 s of Fig. 4, ϕ\phi and −γ-\gamma are in phase to 2.5° (one log sample is 8°). A design that feeds forward only γ̇\dot\gamma would make ϕ\phi lead by 24°. (The amplitudes differ: 0.121 for ϕ\phi against 0.099 for γ\gamma. Section 10 comes back to it.) So the flight used the full vBv_B, as the caption of Fig. 4 in arXiv v1 also writes (ϕ̇p=γ̇−kϕ(ϕ−γ)\dot\phi_p = \dot\gamma - k_\phi(\phi - \gamma)), and its hand adjustment (“since we are inducing γ̇\dot\gamma and not γ\gamma”) is the clock offset and the sign: the hand-adjusted reference of the figure and the logged −γ-\gamma have a correlation of 0.988.

4. Two small slips. The Jacobian of the circle in Section V misses a factor 2 in its second entry (Section 2.1). The same section says that the error decreases “with time constant kϕk_\phi”; kϕk_\phi is the rate, and the time constant is 1/kϕ1/k_\phi = 4 s.

5. A dimension. Section III-B defines γ:ℝ+→ℝn−1\gamma : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1}; it is ℝm−1\mathbb{R}^{m-1}.

Section V-A Jϕ=1r2[2(px−x0)(py−y0)]J_\phi = \frac{1}{r^2}[\,2(p_x - x_0)\ \ (p_y - y_0)\,] 1r2[2(px−x0)2(py−y0)]\frac{1}{r^2}[\,2(p_x - x_0)\ \ 2(p_y - y_0)\,] (item 4)
Section V-A “with time constant kϕk_\phi” rate kϕk_\phi, time constant 1/kϕ1/k_\phi (item 4)
Section III-B γ:ℝ+→ℝn−1\gamma : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1} ℝm−1\mathbb{R}^{m-1} (item 5)

8 The program the aircraft runs

Before take-off, the aircraft knows: the path, as ϕ\phi, ∇ϕ\nabla\phi and HϕH_\phi (here the circle: its centre and radius); the direction ss; the gains kk and kθk_\theta; the behaviour γ(t)\gamma(t), γ̇(t)\dot\gamma(t), γ̈(t)\ddot\gamma(t).

At every tick: read the GPS position pp, the course θ\theta and the ground speed vv; compute ϕ\phi, ∇ϕ\nabla\phi, HϕH_\phi; compute ϑ\vartheta and decide whether it is in Ωb\Omega_b; compute ff (12) and ḟ\dot f; command ω=θ̇c+kθf⊤Eṗ/v2\omega = \dot\theta_c + k_\theta f^\top E\dot p/v^2 to the autopilot. The onboard software uses the measured ground speed as vv, as the paper says, so the field always has the length the aircraft actually flies.

In Python, for the paper’s circle, the whole program is one function. The simulator runs the general version (ik_command in the core below), and on the circle the two agree:

def program(p, theta, v, t, c, r, s, k, kth, A, w):
    """The aircraft, at every tick: position p, course theta, ground speed v, time t -> turn rate omega."""
    dx, dy = p[0] - c[0], p[1] - c[1]
    phi = (dx * dx + dy * dy) / r**2 - 1                         # the error signal
    g = [2 * dx / r**2, 2 * dy / r**2]                           # its gradient; the Hessian is (2/r^2) I
    gam, gamd, gamdd = A * math.sin(w * t), A * w * math.cos(w * t), -A * w * w * math.sin(w * t)
    pd = [v * math.cos(theta), v * math.sin(theta)]
    n2 = g[0] ** 2 + g[1] ** 2
    W = gamd - k * (phi - gam)                                   # the rate the error must have
    th = [g[0] * W / n2, g[1] * W / n2]                          # vartheta = v_C + v_B
    thn = math.hypot(*th)
    Hp = [2 * pd[0] / r**2, 2 * pd[1] / r**2]
    gHp = g[0] * Hp[0] + g[1] * Hp[1]
    Wd = gamdd - k * (g[0] * pd[0] + g[1] * pd[1] - gamd)
    thd = [(Hp[i] - 2 * g[i] * gHp / n2) / n2 * W + g[i] * Wd / n2 for i in range(2)]
    if thn > v:                                                  # outside Omega_b: straight along vartheta
        f = [v * th[0] / thn, v * th[1] / thn]
        q = (th[0] * thd[0] + th[1] * thd[1]) / thn**2
        fd = [v * (thd[i] - th[i] * q) / thn for i in range(2)]
    else:                                                        # inside: the tangent fills the speed
        n = math.sqrt(n2)
        T = [-s * g[1] / n, s * g[0] / n]
        Td0 = [-s * Hp[1], s * Hp[0]]
        q = T[0] * Td0[0] + T[1] * Td0[1]
        Td = [(Td0[i] - T[i] * q) / n for i in range(2)]
        al = math.sqrt(v * v - thn * thn)
        ald = -(th[0] * thd[0] + th[1] * thd[1]) / al if al > 1e-12 else 0.0
        f = [al * T[i] + th[i] for i in range(2)]
        fd = [ald * T[i] + al * Td[i] + thd[i] for i in range(2)]
    thc = (f[0] * fd[1] - f[1] * fd[0]) / v**2                  # the turn rate of the field
    return thc + kth * (f[1] * pd[0] - f[0] * pd[1]) / v**2     # + k_theta f^T E p' / v^2

On 200 random states, program and the simulator’s ik_command differ by at most 4.4e-16 rad/s.

9 The simulator

The world, not the aircraft: the position and the course are integrated with Euler ticks of 10 ms, with ω\omega held during a tick. The wind adds to the airspeed, so the ground speed changes with the course; the program measures it, as the onboard software does. The box below holds the complete core of this page (click to open it).

Notecore.py: the core of this page (click to open; the JavaScript of the figures is a line-by-line port) 
"""The Python core of the paper's pages: every number the explainer prints is computed here, at render time.

Paper: Y. Zhou, J. Bautista, W. Yao, H. Garcia de Marina, "Inverse Kinematics on Guiding Vector Fields for Robot Path
Following", ICRA 2025, arXiv:2502.17313v1. Numbers of equations, figures and remarks are those of arXiv v1.

A line-by-line twin of assets/core.js: same functions, same names, same order of operations. `make check` runs
check() here and EX.core.check() in deno, and compares every value (1e-9). Plain Python (math, lists), no numpy, so
that the port is exact. Vectors are lists [x, y] (or [x, y, z]); E is the rotation by +90 degrees, E [x, y] = [-y, x].

Conventions. The path is the zero level set of phi. The behaviour signal gamma enters as in the paper's (9):
J (v_C + v_B) = gamma' - k (phi - gamma), so that phi -> gamma. (The paper's repository writes e = phi + gamma, so
that phi -> -gamma: the same design with the sign of gamma flipped. The explanation says where it matters.)
"""
import math

G0 = 9.81          # gravity, for the bank angle of a coordinated turn


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ paths in the plane: phi, its gradient, its Hessian
def path(kind, **p):
    """An implicit path phi(p) = 0. kind: circle (r), ellipse (a, b), squircle (a, b), peanut (c, b: a Cassini oval).
    Every kind takes a centre c0 = [x0, y0] and a rotation rot (radians). phi is dimensionless (normalised)."""
    P = {"kind": kind, "c0": [0.0, 0.0], "rot": 0.0}
    P.update(p)
    return P


def level(P, x, y):
    """phi, grad phi = [gx, gy], and the Hessian [hxx, hxy, hyy] at (x, y)."""
    k = P["kind"]
    dx, dy = x - P["c0"][0], y - P["c0"][1]
    if k == "circle":
        r2 = P["r"] * P["r"]
        return (dx * dx + dy * dy) / r2 - 1.0, [2.0 * dx / r2, 2.0 * dy / r2], [2.0 / r2, 0.0, 2.0 / r2]
    ca, sa = math.cos(P["rot"]), math.sin(P["rot"])
    X, Y = ca * dx + sa * dy, -sa * dx + ca * dy           # local coordinates
    if k == "ellipse":
        a2, b2 = P["a"] * P["a"], P["b"] * P["b"]
        phi = X * X / a2 + Y * Y / b2 - 1.0
        gX, gY = 2.0 * X / a2, 2.0 * Y / b2
        hXX, hXY, hYY = 2.0 / a2, 0.0, 2.0 / b2
    elif k == "squircle":
        a4, b4 = P["a"] ** 4, P["b"] ** 4
        phi = X ** 4 / a4 + Y ** 4 / b4 - 1.0
        gX, gY = 4.0 * X ** 3 / a4, 4.0 * Y ** 3 / b4
        hXX, hXY, hYY = 12.0 * X * X / a4, 0.0, 12.0 * Y * Y / b4
    elif k == "peanut":                                      # ((X^2+Y^2)^2 - 2c^2(X^2-Y^2) + c^4) / b^4 - 1
        c2, b4 = P["c"] * P["c"], P["b"] ** 4
        q = X * X + Y * Y
        phi = (q * q - 2.0 * c2 * (X * X - Y * Y) + c2 * c2) / b4 - 1.0
        gX, gY = (4.0 * q * X - 4.0 * c2 * X) / b4, (4.0 * q * Y + 4.0 * c2 * Y) / b4
        hXX = (4.0 * q + 8.0 * X * X - 4.0 * c2) / b4
        hXY = 8.0 * X * Y / b4
        hYY = (4.0 * q + 8.0 * Y * Y + 4.0 * c2) / b4
    else:
        raise ValueError(k)
    # back to the world frame: g = R gl, H = R Hl R^T
    gx, gy = ca * gX - sa * gY, sa * gX + ca * gY
    hxx = ca * ca * hXX - 2.0 * ca * sa * hXY + sa * sa * hYY
    hxy = ca * sa * hXX + (ca * ca - sa * sa) * hXY - ca * sa * hYY
    hyy = sa * sa * hXX + 2.0 * ca * sa * hXY + ca * ca * hYY
    return phi, [gx, gy], [hxx, hxy, hyy]


def circle_radial_error(phi, r):
    """The paper's Section V: on the normalised circle phi = rho^2/r^2 - 1, the radial error is r sqrt(phi + 1) - r."""
    return r * math.sqrt(phi + 1.0) - r


def omega_b_circle(r, v, k):
    """The annulus where |v_C| <= v for u_phi = -k phi on the normalised circle (no gamma): |v_C| = k |rho^2 - r^2| / (2 rho).
    Returns its inner and outer radii."""
    q = v / k
    return -q + math.sqrt(q * q + r * r), q + math.sqrt(q * q + r * r)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the behaviour signal gamma(t), with two derivatives
def gamma(spec, t):
    """[gamma, gamma', gamma''] at time t. spec kinds: none; sine (A, w, ph); fourier (w0, a: [a0, a1, ...], b: [0, b1, ...]),
    a periodic signal drawn by the reader; hold (g, gd): a value and a rate held by the keys (gamma'' = 0)."""
    k = spec["kind"]
    if k == "none":
        return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
    if k == "sine":
        A, w, ph = spec["A"], spec["w"], spec.get("ph", 0.0)
        s, c = math.sin(w * t + ph), math.cos(w * t + ph)
        return [A * s, A * w * c, -A * w * w * s]
    if k == "fourier":
        w0, a, b = spec["w0"], spec["a"], spec["b"]
        g, gd, gdd = a[0], 0.0, 0.0
        for m in range(1, len(a)):
            c, s = math.cos(m * w0 * t), math.sin(m * w0 * t)
            g += a[m] * c + b[m] * s
            gd += m * w0 * (-a[m] * s + b[m] * c)
            gdd += -(m * w0) * (m * w0) * (a[m] * c + b[m] * s)
        return [g, gd, gdd]
    if k == "hold":
        return [spec["g"], spec["gd"], 0.0]
    raise ValueError(k)


def fourier_fit(vals, K):
    """The harmonics 0..K of a periodic signal sampled at m equally spaced times over one period: a, b for gamma()."""
    m = len(vals)
    a, b = [], []
    for k in range(K + 1):
        sa, sb = 0.0, 0.0
        for i in range(m):
            ang = 2.0 * math.pi * k * i / m
            sa += vals[i] * math.cos(ang)
            sb += vals[i] * math.sin(ang)
        if k == 0:
            a.append(sa / m)
            b.append(0.0)
        else:
            a.append(2.0 * sa / m)
            b.append(2.0 * sb / m)
    return a, b


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ single integrators in the plane (Sections II and III)
def ik_si(P, p, k, vt, s, gm, full=True):
    """The IK-GVF (8) with the behaviour term (9): f = v_T + v_C + v_B, v_T = s vt E grad/|grad| (a tangential speed vt),
    J (v_C + v_B) = gamma' - k (phi - gamma). full=False drops the k gamma term (only gamma' is fed forward)."""
    phi, g, H = level(P, p[0], p[1])
    n2 = g[0] * g[0] + g[1] * g[1]
    n = math.sqrt(n2)
    w = gm[1] - k * (phi - gm[0]) if full else gm[1] - k * phi
    return [s * vt * -g[1] / n + g[0] * w / n2, s * vt * g[0] / n + g[1] * w / n2], phi


def classic_si(P, p, k, vt, s):
    """The classic field of the paper's Example 1 and Remark 1, with the same tangential part: s vt E grad/|grad| - k phi grad."""
    phi, g, H = level(P, p[0], p[1])
    n = math.sqrt(g[0] * g[0] + g[1] * g[1])
    return [s * vt * -g[1] / n - k * phi * g[0], s * vt * g[0] / n - k * phi * g[1]], phi


def run_si(P, p0, field, k, vt, s, dt, steps, gspec=None, every=1, full=True):
    """A single integrator p' = f(p, t), Euler ticks of a held command. Returns [[t, x, y, phi], ...]."""
    gspec = gspec or {"kind": "none"}
    p = [p0[0], p0[1]]
    out = []
    for j in range(steps + 1):
        t = j * dt
        if field == "ik":
            f, phi = ik_si(P, p, k, vt, s, gamma(gspec, t), full)
        else:
            f, phi = classic_si(P, p, k, vt, s)
        if j % every == 0:
            out.append([t, p[0], p[1], phi])
        p = [p[0] + dt * f[0], p[1] + dt * f[1]]
    return out


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the fixed-wing: the field (12) and the heading law (13)
def ik_command(P, st, v, prm, gm):
    """What the aircraft computes at every tick. st = {x, y, psi}: its position and its course; v: its ground speed
    (the onboard software uses the GPS speed); prm = {k, kth, s, full}; gm = [gamma, gamma', gamma''].
    Returns the field f (12), its time derivative along the motion, the heading rate omega (13) and the pieces."""
    k, s = prm["k"], prm["s"]
    pdx, pdy = v * math.cos(st["psi"]), v * math.sin(st["psi"])          # p' = v R(psi) p0
    phi, g, H = level(P, st["x"], st["y"])
    n2 = g[0] * g[0] + g[1] * g[1]
    if not n2 > 1e-24:                                                   # a critical point of phi: no field, fly on
        return {"omega": 0.0, "thc": 0.0, "f": [pdx, pdy], "fd": [0.0, 0.0], "phi": phi, "alpha": 0.0, "theta": 0.0,
                "inside": False, "fEp": 0.0, "alphadot": 0.0}
    n = math.sqrt(n2)
    full = prm.get("full", True)
    # vartheta = v_C + v_B = beta w, with beta = grad / |grad|^2 and w = gamma' - k (phi - gamma)
    w = gm[1] - k * (phi - gm[0]) if full else gm[1] - k * phi
    th = [g[0] * w / n2, g[1] * w / n2]
    thn = math.sqrt(th[0] * th[0] + th[1] * th[1])
    # its time derivative along the motion: beta' w + beta w'
    phid = g[0] * pdx + g[1] * pdy
    wd = gm[2] - k * (phid - gm[1]) if full else gm[2] - k * phid
    Hp = [H[0] * pdx + H[1] * pdy, H[1] * pdx + H[2] * pdy]
    gHp = g[0] * Hp[0] + g[1] * Hp[1]
    bd = [Hp[0] / n2 - 2.0 * g[0] * gHp / (n2 * n2), Hp[1] / n2 - 2.0 * g[1] * gHp / (n2 * n2)]
    thd = [bd[0] * w + g[0] * wd / n2, bd[1] * w + g[1] * wd / n2]
    T = [s * -g[1] / n, s * g[0] / n]                                    # the unit tangent, s E grad / |grad|
    if thn > v:                                                          # outside Omega_b: straight along vartheta
        inside, alpha, ad = False, 0.0, 0.0
        f = [v * th[0] / thn, v * th[1] / thn]
        tt = (th[0] * thd[0] + th[1] * thd[1]) / (thn * thn)
        fd = [v * (thd[0] - th[0] * tt) / thn, v * (thd[1] - th[1] * tt) / thn]
    else:
        inside = True
        alpha = math.sqrt(v * v - thn * thn)
        vTd = [s * -Hp[1], s * Hp[0]]                                    # d/dt (s E grad) = s E H p'
        tv = T[0] * vTd[0] + T[1] * vTd[1]
        Td = [(vTd[0] - T[0] * tv) / n, (vTd[1] - T[1] * tv) / n]
        ad = -(th[0] * thd[0] + th[1] * thd[1]) / alpha if alpha > 1e-12 else 0.0
        f = [alpha * T[0] + th[0], alpha * T[1] + th[1]]
        fd = [ad * T[0] + alpha * Td[0] + thd[0], ad * T[1] + alpha * Td[1] + thd[1]]
    if prm.get("fdot") == "paper":                                       # the paper's printed f', to measure it
        fd = paper_fd(P, st, v, prm, gm, f, alpha, ad, inside)
    thc = (f[0] * fd[1] - f[1] * fd[0]) / (v * v)                       # f^T E^T f' / v^2: the turn rate of f
    fEp = -f[0] * pdy + f[1] * pdx                                       # f^T E p'
    om = thc + prm["kth"] * fEp / (v * v)
    return {"omega": om, "thc": thc, "f": f, "fd": fd, "phi": phi, "alpha": alpha, "theta": thn, "inside": inside,
            "fEp": fEp, "alphadot": ad}


def classic_command(P, st, v, prm, gm=None):
    """The classic field for the same aircraft: chi = s E grad - ke phi grad, flown at the speed v, f = v chi/|chi|,
    with the same heading law (13). prm = {ke, kth, s}."""
    ke, s = prm["ke"], prm["s"]
    pdx, pdy = v * math.cos(st["psi"]), v * math.sin(st["psi"])
    phi, g, H = level(P, st["x"], st["y"])
    chi = [s * -g[1] - ke * phi * g[0], s * g[0] - ke * phi * g[1]]
    cn = math.sqrt(chi[0] * chi[0] + chi[1] * chi[1])
    if not cn > 1e-12:                                                   # a singular point of the classic field
        return {"omega": 0.0, "thc": 0.0, "f": [pdx, pdy], "fd": [0.0, 0.0], "phi": phi, "alpha": 0.0, "theta": 0.0,
                "inside": False, "fEp": 0.0, "alphadot": 0.0}
    Hp = [H[0] * pdx + H[1] * pdy, H[1] * pdx + H[2] * pdy]
    phid = g[0] * pdx + g[1] * pdy
    chid = [s * -Hp[1] - ke * phi * Hp[0] - ke * phid * g[0], s * Hp[0] - ke * phi * Hp[1] - ke * phid * g[1]]
    f = [v * chi[0] / cn, v * chi[1] / cn]
    cc = (chi[0] * chid[0] + chi[1] * chid[1]) / (cn * cn)
    fd = [v * (chid[0] - chi[0] * cc) / cn, v * (chid[1] - chi[1] * cc) / cn]
    thc = (f[0] * fd[1] - f[1] * fd[0]) / (v * v)
    fEp = -f[0] * pdy + f[1] * pdx
    om = thc + prm["kth"] * fEp / (v * v)
    return {"omega": om, "thc": thc, "f": f, "fd": fd, "phi": phi, "alpha": 0.0, "theta": 0.0, "inside": True,
            "fEp": fEp, "alphadot": 0.0}


def paper_fd(P, st, v, prm, gm, f, al, ad, inside):
    """The expressions for f' after Theorem 2 in arXiv:2502.17313v1, taken literally, with v_T = s E grad as in
    Section V: zero outside Omega_b (as its text says), and alpha' v_T/|v_T| + alpha (I/|v_T| - v_T v_T^T/|v_T|^3) v_T'
    + vartheta' inside, with beta' as printed (p' in its first term and f in the last one). Selected by
    prm["fdot"] = "paper", to measure its effect."""
    if not inside:
        return [0.0, 0.0]
    k, s = prm["k"], prm["s"]
    pdx, pdy = v * math.cos(st["psi"]), v * math.sin(st["psi"])
    phi, g, H = level(P, st["x"], st["y"])
    n2 = g[0] * g[0] + g[1] * g[1]
    n = math.sqrt(n2)
    w = gm[1] - k * (phi - gm[0])
    Hp = [H[0] * pdx + H[1] * pdy, H[1] * pdx + H[2] * pdy]
    pHg = g[0] * Hp[0] + g[1] * Hp[1]                                    # p'^T H J^T
    Hf = [H[0] * f[0] + H[1] * f[1], H[1] * f[0] + H[2] * f[1]]
    gHf = g[0] * Hf[0] + g[1] * Hf[1]                                    # J H^T f
    bd = [(Hp[0] - g[0] / n2 * (pHg + gHf)) / n2, (Hp[1] - g[1] / n2 * (pHg + gHf)) / n2]
    phid = g[0] * pdx + g[1] * pdy
    wd = gm[2] - k * (phid - gm[1])
    thd = [bd[0] * w + g[0] * wd / n2, bd[1] * w + g[1] * wd / n2]
    vT = [s * -g[1], s * g[0]]
    vTd = [s * -Hp[1], s * Hp[0]]
    vv = vT[0] * vTd[0] + vT[1] * vTd[1]
    fd = [ad * vT[0] / n + al * (vTd[0] / n - vT[0] * vv / (n * n * n)) + thd[0],
          ad * vT[1] / n + al * (vTd[1] / n - vT[1] * vv / (n * n * n)) + thd[1]]
    return fd


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the world: a unicycle at constant airspeed, in a wind
def ground_speed(psi, va, wind):
    """The ground speed along the course psi, for an airspeed va and a wind (wx, wy) slower than va."""
    hw = math.cos(psi) * wind[0] + math.sin(psi) * wind[1]
    return hw + math.sqrt(va * va - wind[0] * wind[0] - wind[1] * wind[1] + hw * hw)


def sat(x, m):
    return x if m <= 0 else max(-m, min(m, x))


def tick(st, v, om, dt):
    """The world: one tick of (10) with the turn rate om and the speed v held, so the aircraft flies an arc (exact for a
    held command; a straight segment when om = 0)."""
    a = om * dt
    if abs(a) > 1e-9:
        return {"x": st["x"] + v * (math.sin(st["psi"] + a) - math.sin(st["psi"])) / om,
                "y": st["y"] + v * (math.cos(st["psi"]) - math.cos(st["psi"] + a)) / om, "psi": st["psi"] + a}
    return {"x": st["x"] + dt * v * math.cos(st["psi"]), "y": st["y"] + dt * v * math.sin(st["psi"]), "psi": st["psi"] + a}


def fly(P, st0, prm, va, wind, dt, steps, gspec=None, mode="ik", umax=0.0, every=1):
    """Fly the aircraft (10) for `steps` ticks with the commands held. The course turns at omega, saturated at
    umax (0: no limit). The program measures its ground speed v and uses it as the paper's v (the onboard choice).
    Returns rows [t, x, y, psi, phi, omega, thc, alpha, |vartheta|, gamma, inside]."""
    gspec = gspec or {"kind": "none"}
    st = {"x": st0["x"], "y": st0["y"], "psi": st0["psi"]}
    out = []
    for j in range(steps + 1):
        t = j * dt
        v = ground_speed(st["psi"], va, wind)
        gm = gamma(gspec, t)
        c = ik_command(P, st, v, prm, gm) if mode == "ik" else classic_command(P, st, v, prm, gm)
        if j % every == 0:
            out.append([t, st["x"], st["y"], st["psi"], c["phi"], c["omega"], c["thc"], c["alpha"], c["theta"], gm[0],
                        1.0 if c["inside"] else 0.0])
        st = tick(st, v, sat(c["omega"], umax), dt)
    return out


def bank(omega, v):
    """The bank angle of a coordinated turn at the rate omega and the speed v: atan(v omega / g), in degrees."""
    return math.atan(v * omega / G0) * 180.0 / math.pi


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ three dimensions: a path as two surfaces (m = 3)
def level3(kind, r, h, q):
    """phi = [phi_1, phi_2] and the Jacobian J (2 x 3) of three paths in R^3, each the intersection of two surfaces:
    ring (the cylinder x^2+y^2 = r^2 and the tilted plane z = h x / r), saddle (the cylinder and z = h (x^2-y^2)/r^2),
    viviani (the sphere |q|^2 = 4 r^2 and the cylinder (x-r)^2 + y^2 = r^2, tangent at (2r, 0, 0))."""
    x, y, z = q
    r2 = r * r
    if kind == "viviani":
        p1 = (x * x + y * y + z * z) / (4.0 * r2) - 1.0
        g1 = [x / (2.0 * r2), y / (2.0 * r2), z / (2.0 * r2)]
        p2 = ((x - r) * (x - r) + y * y) / r2 - 1.0
        g2 = [2.0 * (x - r) / r2, 2.0 * y / r2, 0.0]
        return [p1, p2], [g1, g2]
    p1 = (x * x + y * y) / r2 - 1.0
    g1 = [2.0 * x / r2, 2.0 * y / r2, 0.0]
    if kind == "ring":
        p2 = (z - h * x / r) / r
        g2 = [-h / r2, 0.0, 1.0 / r]
    else:
        p2 = (z - h * (x * x - y * y) / r2) / r
        g2 = [-2.0 * h * x / (r2 * r), 2.0 * h * y / (r2 * r), 1.0 / r]
    return [p1, p2], [g1, g2]


def ik3(kind, r, h, q, K, vt):
    """The IK-GVF (8) in R^3 with u_phi = -K phi (K = [k1, k2]): f = vt t_hat + J^T (J J^T)^-1 u, t_hat along
    grad phi_1 x grad phi_2 (the kernel of J). Returns f, phi and det(J J^T); f is None where J J^T is singular."""
    phi, J = level3(kind, r, h, q)
    a = J[0][0] * J[0][0] + J[0][1] * J[0][1] + J[0][2] * J[0][2]
    b = J[0][0] * J[1][0] + J[0][1] * J[1][1] + J[0][2] * J[1][2]
    c = J[1][0] * J[1][0] + J[1][1] * J[1][1] + J[1][2] * J[1][2]
    det = a * c - b * b
    cr = [J[0][1] * J[1][2] - J[0][2] * J[1][1], J[0][2] * J[1][0] - J[0][0] * J[1][2], J[0][0] * J[1][1] - J[0][1] * J[1][0]]
    cn = math.sqrt(cr[0] * cr[0] + cr[1] * cr[1] + cr[2] * cr[2])
    if det <= 1e-14 * (a * c) or cn == 0.0:
        return None, phi, det
    u = [-K[0] * phi[0], -K[1] * phi[1]]
    l1, l2 = (c * u[0] - b * u[1]) / det, (-b * u[0] + a * u[1]) / det     # (J J^T)^-1 u
    f = [vt * cr[i] / cn + J[0][i] * l1 + J[1][i] * l2 for i in range(3)]
    return f, phi, det


def run3(kind, r, h, q0, K, vt, dt, steps, every=1, vmax=0.0):
    """A single integrator in R^3 on the IK-GVF. vmax > 0 caps the speed (as a real robot would). A singular point stops
    the robot. Returns rows [t, x, y, z, phi_1, phi_2, det]."""
    q = q0[:]
    out = []
    for j in range(steps + 1):
        f, phi, det = ik3(kind, r, h, q, K, vt)
        if j % every == 0:
            out.append([j * dt, q[0], q[1], q[2], phi[0], phi[1], det])
        if f is None:
            continue
        if vmax > 0:
            fn = math.sqrt(f[0] * f[0] + f[1] * f[1] + f[2] * f[2])
            if fn > vmax:
                f = [vmax * f[0] / fn, vmax * f[1] / fn, vmax * f[2] / fn]
        q = [q[0] + dt * f[0], q[1] + dt * f[1], q[2] + dt * f[2]]
    return out


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the paper's flights (Section V), as set onboard
R_PAPER = 100.0                     # the circle's radius, m
CIRCLE = path("circle", r=R_PAPER)
VA = 15.0                           # the airspeed; the flights logged ground speeds of 14 to 17 m/s
WIND = [-1.73, 1.0]                 # "around 2 m/s" (towards 150 degrees: the logged ground speed is 17 m/s at the start)
DT = 0.01
FLIGHT1 = {"k": 0.25, "kth": 0.6, "s": -1.0}                   # Fig. 3 (exp1)
FLIGHT2 = {"k": 0.25, "kth": 0.8, "s": -1.0}                   # Fig. 4 (exp2) and Fig. 2 (exp3)
START1 = {"x": 225.45, "y": -231.45, "psi": 149.0 * math.pi / 180.0}   # Fig. 3: the logged start, from the centre
WIGGLE2 = {"kind": "sine", "A": 0.1, "w": 0.55}
WIGGLE3 = {"kind": "sine", "A": 0.03, "w": 1.3}
PEANUT = path("peanut", c=80.0, b=92.0)
SQUIRCLE = path("squircle", a=110.0, b=110.0)
ELLIPSE = path("ellipse", a=150.0, b=80.0, rot=0.3)


def check():
    """The same keys as EX.core.check() in assets/core.js."""
    out = {}
    pts = [[37.0, -120.0], [-150.0, 44.0]]
    for nm, P in [("circle", CIRCLE), ("ellipse", ELLIPSE), ("squircle", SQUIRCLE), ("peanut", PEANUT)]:
        vals = []
        for q in pts:
            phi, g, H = level(P, q[0], q[1])
            vals += [phi] + g + H
        out["level_" + nm] = vals
    out["omegab"] = list(omega_b_circle(R_PAPER, 15.0, 0.25)) + [circle_radial_error(0.1, R_PAPER)]
    out["gamma"] = gamma(WIGGLE2, 3.7) + gamma({"kind": "fourier", "w0": 0.3, "a": [0.01, 0.05, -0.02], "b": [0.0, 0.03, 0.04]}, 2.2)
    a, b = fourier_fit([math.sin(2 * math.pi * i / 64) + 0.3 * math.cos(6 * math.pi * i / 64) for i in range(64)], 4)
    out["fourier"] = a + b
    r1 = run_si(ELLIPSE, [260.0, 40.0], "ik", 0.4, 10.0, 1.0, 0.01, 1500, every=500)
    r2 = run_si(ELLIPSE, [260.0, 40.0], "classic", 4000.0, 10.0, 1.0, 0.01, 1500, every=500)
    r3 = run_si(CIRCLE, [130.0, 0.0], "ik", 0.5, 10.0, -1.0, 0.01, 1500, WIGGLE2, every=500, full=False)
    out["si"] = [x for row in r1 + r2 + r3 for x in row]
    st = {"x": 40.0, "y": -30.0, "psi": 2.0}
    c = ik_command(PEANUT, st, 15.0, FLIGHT2, gamma(WIGGLE2, 1.0))
    out["cmd"] = [c["omega"], c["thc"], c["alpha"], c["theta"]] + c["f"] + c["fd"]
    c = classic_command(SQUIRCLE, st, 15.0, {"ke": 3.0, "kth": 0.8, "s": -1.0})
    out["cmd_classic"] = [c["omega"], c["thc"]] + c["f"] + c["fd"]
    c = ik_command(CIRCLE, {"x": 60.0, "y": 90.0, "psi": 0.4}, 15.0, dict(FLIGHT2, fdot="paper"), gamma(WIGGLE2, 1.0))
    out["paper_fdot"] = c["fd"] + [c["omega"]]
    st1 = {"x": -320.0, "y": -60.0, "psi": 0.5}
    run = fly(CIRCLE, st1, FLIGHT1, VA, WIND, DT, 3000, umax=1.2, every=600)
    out["fly1"] = [x for row in run for x in row]
    run = fly(PEANUT, {"x": 20.0, "y": 10.0, "psi": 1.0}, FLIGHT2, VA, [1.5, 0.0], DT, 3000, WIGGLE2, every=600)
    out["fly2"] = [x for row in run for x in row]
    run = fly(SQUIRCLE, st1, {"ke": 2.0, "kth": 0.8, "s": 1.0}, VA, [0.0, 0.0], DT, 3000, mode="classic", every=600)
    out["fly_classic"] = [x for row in run for x in row]
    run = run3("saddle", 50.0, 20.0, [70.0, -20.0, 30.0], [0.3, 0.8], 8.0, 0.01, 2000, every=500)
    out["run3"] = [x for row in run for x in row]
    run = run3("viviani", 50.0, 0.0, [80.0, 30.0, 40.0], [0.4, 0.4], 8.0, 0.01, 1000, every=250, vmax=20.0)
    out["run3v"] = [x for row in run for x in row]
    out["bank"] = [bank(0.71, 16.6)]
    out["tick"] = list(tick({"x": 1.0, "y": 2.0, "psi": 0.3}, 15.0, 0.4, 0.01).values()) + list(tick({"x": 1.0, "y": 2.0, "psi": 0.3}, 15.0, 0.0, 0.01).values())
    return out

10 Running it: the paper’s flights again

The paper’s repository keeps the telemetry logs of the flights. This page reads them (the windows that drew the paper’s figures, data/README.md) and runs the same flights in the simulator: airspeed 15 m/s, a wind of 2 m/s (the paper says “around 2 m/s”; the direction is chosen to match the logged 17 m/s at the start of flight 1), and the paper’s gains. The logs arrive at 4 Hz, and positions at about 1 Hz.

10.1 Flight 1: the designed transient (the paper’s Fig. 3)

The aircraft starts at ϕ\phi = 9.44, about 323 m from the centre. Outside Ωb\Omega_b it flies straight in; the log shows ∥vT∥=α=0\|v_T\| = \alpha = 0 there, as (12) says. The log enters Ωb\Omega_b at 8.25 s (the paper marks 8 s), the simulation at 8.00 s. Then ϕ\phi decays. Fitted over the next 12 s, the log decays at 0.244 and the simulation at 0.252, for a designed k=0.25k = 0.25. The largest gap between the log and the paper’s prediction ϕp\phi_p (from 8 s) is 0.23, in the simulation 0.016: the wind, the 1 Hz positions and the aircraft’s own roll dynamics are not in the model.

10.2 Flight 2: the oscillation (the paper’s Fig. 4)

The simulation flies γ=−Asin⁡(wt)\gamma = -A\sin(wt) in the paper’s convention, which is the repository’s +Asin⁡(wt)+A\sin(wt) (item 3 of Section 7), with A=0.1A = 0.1, w=0.55w = 0.55 rad/s and kθ=0.8k_\theta = 0.8. Its ϕ\phi has an amplitude of 0.100 and follows γ\gamma to 0.0021. The log’s ϕ\phi is in phase with its −γ-\gamma, but swings 22 % more: an amplitude of 0.121. The model does not explain this. The wind of the model is steady, and the real aircraft’s roll lags the commanded ω\omega; either can add to the swing [open]. In metres, the radial gap between where the log’s ϕ\phi puts the aircraft and where −γ-\gamma asks for has an RMS of 2.0 m and a maximum of 4.3 m, which is the paper’s “around 5 meters”. The log’s ∥vC∥\|v_C\| swings between about 0 and 3 m/s, as in the paper’s figure and in the simulation.

10.3 Flight 3: telemetry with and without the oscillation (the paper’s Fig. 2)

The paper’s motivation is telemetry. In the third flight the drone is far from the ground station, and the station receives positions only from time to time. With an oscillation of A=0.03A = 0.03 (about 1.5 m) at w=1.3w = 1.3 rad/s, the paper’s Fig. 2 shows the received positions more evenly spread over the circle than without it. The logs say the same, mildly. Counting the position messages that arrived while the drone was on the circle:

with the oscillation without
time on the circle 110 s (2.7 laps) 98 s (2.4 laps)
positions received 68 (0.62 per s) 56 (0.57 per s)
largest arc of the circle with no position 20° 38°
longest silence 8.5 s 7.8 s
spread (standard deviation) of the bank angle 14.0° 4.2°

The oscillation does what it is meant to do to the roll: the bank angle moves about three times as much. The reception is somewhat better, and its largest hole is half as wide. This is one flight of each, about two minutes, so it is an observation and not a statistic [numerical].

11 What changes elsewhere, and what this page does not cover

Other paths. Nothing in Steps 2 to 5 is special to the circle. The field needs ∇ϕ≠0\nabla\phi \neq 0 near the path, and the aircraft needs Ωb\Omega_b to contain a neighbourhood of it. The playground flies an ellipse, a rounded square and a peanut-shaped oval. Theorem 1 holds on each wherever the heading is aligned [proved]. How well a real aircraft stays aligned on a tight curve depends on kθk_\theta and its turn limit [numerical].

More dimensions. Theorem 1 is stated for any mm [proved]; Section 3.2 shows one single-integrator example with m=3m = 3. The paper’s constant-speed field (12) and Theorem 2 are for the plane. An aircraft that also climbs is not covered.

Not covered here.

  • The wind as the paper handles it: the onboard software sets vv to the GPS speed. The simulator does the same, and ignores v̇\dot v in ḟ\dot f, as the onboard software does. Theorem 2 assumes a constant vv.
  • Turn limits. The simulator commands ω\omega without a limit unless a figure says so. The aircraft has one.
  • Several aircraft. The paper’s repository simulates three drones on the same path with different oscillations; they do not coordinate. The playground shows them.
  • Paths with crossings. There ∇ϕ=0\nabla\phi = 0 on the path and Assumption 2 fails; the singularity-free field of the lab’s TRO 2021 paper is the tool for those.

12 Glossary

pp, θ\theta, vv, ω\omega
the position, the course, the ground speed and the commanded turn rate of the aircraft.
ϕ\phi, ∇ϕ\nabla\phi, HϕH_\phi, JϕJ_\phi
the error signal (the path is ϕ=0\phi = 0), its gradient, its Hessian, and its Jacobian (Jϕ=∇ϕ⊤J_\phi = \nabla\phi^\top in the plane).
EE, ss
the rotation by +90°+90°, and the direction of travel (s=−1s = -1: clockwise, as in the flights).
vTv_T, v̂T\hat v_T
the tangential part of the field, sE∇ϕs E\nabla\phi, and its unit vector.
uϕu_\phi, kk
the designed rate of the error, here uϕ=−kϕu_\phi = -k\phi; kk is its rate (the paper’s kϕk_\phi and kBk_B).
vCv_C, vBv_B, β\beta, ϑ\vartheta
the converging and the behaviour parts, β=Jϕ⊤(JϕJϕ⊤)−1\beta = J_\phi^\top(J_\phi J_\phi^\top)^{-1}, and ϑ=vC+vB\vartheta = v_C + v_B.
γ(t)\gamma(t), AA, ww
the behaviour signal that ϕ\phi follows, and the amplitude and frequency of its sine.
α\alpha, Ωb\Omega_b
the tangential speed v2−∥ϑ∥2\sqrt{v^2 - \|\vartheta\|^2}, and the set where ∥ϑ∥≤v\|\vartheta\| \le v.
θ̇c\dot\theta_c, kθk_\theta
the turn rate of the field along the motion, and the gain of the heading feedback (Theorem 2).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**From the [Swarm Systems Lab](https://www.swarmsystemslab.eu/publications/inverse-kinematics-on-guiding-vector-fields-for-robot-path-following),** University of Granada. To try the results by hand, open the
[playground](playground.html).

**What this page does.** It takes the paper *Inverse Kinematics on Guiding Vector Fields for Robot Path Following*
(ICRA 2025, [arXiv:2502.17313](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17313) v1) and writes it out for the paper's own example: a circle of radius 100 m, flown by a
fixed-wing drone at about 15 m/s. It goes step by step: the error signal of a path and the classic guiding field
(Section II of the paper), the inverse-kinematics field that makes the error obey a linear system (Lemma 1 and
Theorem 1), the oscillation added on purpose around the path (Section III-B), the field for an aircraft that cannot
change its speed (Section IV), and the heading law that tracks it (Theorem 2). It ends with the program the aircraft
runs, and with the paper's three flights, simulated again and compared with their logs.

**Source and status.** The results are the paper's, and this page does not re-prove them. It adds four things, each
marked where it appears: a comparison with the classic field when the path changes size (@sec-ik), a
three-dimensional example (@sec-m3), a check of the formulas after Theorem 2 against the exact derivative, which finds
where they differ (@sec-checks), and a reading of the flight logs of the paper's repository (@sec-flights).
Equation, figure and remark numbers are those of arXiv v1, the ICRA version. Where this page departs from it
because arXiv v1 is not correct, @sec-errata says so. Every
number on the page is computed by `core.py` when the page is rendered. The interactive figures run
`assets/core.js`, and `make check` proves that the two agree.
:::

# The problem

A small fixed-wing drone flies at a constant height. Its horizontal position is $p = (p_x, p_y)$ and its course is
$\theta$. It cannot stop or slow down: its speed $v$ is fixed by the airspeed (and changed by the wind). The only
command is the turn rate $\omega$. This is the paper's model (10):

$$
\dot p = v \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \dot\theta = \omega .
$$

**What it measures.** Its own position and ground velocity (GPS), so also $v$ and $\theta$. Nothing else. There is
one aircraft and no communication.

**The path.** A closed curve given by an implicit equation $\phi(p) = 0$. The paper's flights use a circle of radius
$r = 100$ m around a centre $c$, normalised so that $\phi$ has no units:

$$
\phi(p) = \frac{\|p - c\|^2}{r^2} - 1 .
$$

So $\phi = 0$ on the circle, $\phi < 0$ inside and $\phi > 0$ outside. The number $\phi(p)$ is the *error signal*:
it is what the aircraft drives to zero. It is not a distance. With $\rho = \|p - c\|$, $\phi = \rho^2/r^2 - 1$, and
a radial error of $\rho - r$ metres reads $\phi \approx 2(\rho - r)/r$. The paper's Section V gives the exact
conversion, $\rho - r = r\sqrt{\phi + 1} - r$: $\phi = 0.1$ is `{python} f2(circle_radial_error(0.1, R))` m outside
and $\phi = -0.1$ is `{python} f2(-circle_radial_error(-0.1, R))` m inside.

**The task.** Follow the path, and choose *how* the aircraft gets there: how fast the error decays, and what it does
around the path. The paper's motivation is concrete. The drone's dipole antenna radiates badly in some directions,
and the bank angle of a long turn can keep it pointed the wrong way for a while. A small, controlled oscillation
around the path changes the bank angle all the time. Shaking the roll directly would leave the path; the paper puts
the oscillation into $\phi$ instead, where it has a meaning in metres and stays inside a closed loop.

**Why it is hard.** Classic guiding fields make $\phi$ go to zero, but how fast depends on the gradient of $\phi$,
so on the path, its scale and its normalisation. And an aircraft at constant speed cannot obey a field whose length
changes.

# Step 1: the error signal and the classic field

## What $\phi$ tells the robot {#sec-phi}

For a robot in the plane ($m = 2$, the paper writes the general case $p \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with $m - 1$ functions
$\phi_i$), the chain rule gives the paper's (1):

$$
\dot\phi = J_\phi(p)\,\dot p, \qquad J_\phi = \nabla\phi^\top .
$$

For the circle, with $d = p - c$,

$$
\nabla\phi(p) = \frac{2}{r^2}\, d, \qquad H_\phi = \frac{2}{r^2} I_2 .
$$

(arXiv v1 prints $J_\phi = \tfrac{1}{r^2}[\,2(p_x - x_0),\ (p_y - y_0)\,]$ in Section V; the second entry misses its
factor 2, @sec-errata.) On the path $\|\nabla\phi\| = 2/r$ = `{python} f3(2 / R)` per metre. Moving along the level set
does not change $\phi$: the velocities with $J_\phi v_T = 0$ are the multiples of $E\nabla\phi$, with
$E = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$ the rotation by $90°$. That is the paper's
tangent space $T_p(\mathcal{M}_{\phi_z})$, of dimension one. The paper needs $\nabla\phi \neq 0$ near the path
(Assumption 2). For the circle it fails only at the centre.

```{=html}
<div id="ex-level" class="column-body"></div><script>EX.figs.wLevel("ex-level")</script>
```

## The classic field

The paper's Example 1 is the classic guiding vector field,

$$
f(p) = v_T - J_\phi^\top \phi = s\,E\nabla\phi - k\,\phi\,\nabla\phi, \qquad s = \pm 1 ,
$$

(Remark 1, with a gain $k$; $s$ chooses the direction of travel). A robot that follows it exactly has
$\dot\phi = -k\,\|\nabla\phi\|^2\,\phi$. That converges, by the Lyapunov function $V = \phi^2/2$ of Example 1, but
the rate is $k\|\nabla\phi\|^2$, and it changes with the place, the path and the way $\phi$ is written.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rate_classic_100 = 4 / R**2
rate_classic_400 = 4 / 400**2
```

On the paper's circle, $\|\nabla\phi\|^2 = 4\rho^2/r^4$. On the path it is `{python} e1(rate_classic_100)` per square
metre. So with $k = 1$ the error decays at `{python} e1(rate_classic_100)` per second, a time constant of
`{python} f0(1 / rate_classic_100)` s. Fly a circle of 400 m with the same $k$ and the rate falls 16 times. The gain
of the classic field must be retuned for every path.

**Singular points.** Where $f = 0$ the robot stops; where the field is normalised, its direction is undefined. The
paper calls this set $\Psi$ (4) and shows that a guiding field needs $J_\phi$ of full rank near the path
(Proposition 1). For the circle the classic field vanishes only at the centre.

# Step 2: inverse kinematics on the error {#sec-ik}

## The field

The paper asks for more than convergence: it wants $\dot\phi = u_\phi$ for an input $u_\phi$ it designs (Problem 1).
Split the field in two, $f = v_T + v_C$, with $v_T$ along the level set. Then $\dot\phi = J_\phi v_C$, and the
paper picks $v_C$ by inverse kinematics, the least-norm solution of $J_\phi v_C = u_\phi$ (the paper's (7) and (8)):

$$
v_C = J_\phi^\top\left(J_\phi J_\phi^\top\right)^{-1} u_\phi
\;\overset{m = 2}{=}\; \frac{\nabla\phi}{\|\nabla\phi\|^2}\, u_\phi .
$$

This is what a robot arm does with its end effector, applied to the error of a path: the Jacobian's pseudo-inverse
turns a desired rate of the error into a velocity.

**Lemma 1.** $v_T$ and $v_C$ are orthogonal ($v_T^\top v_C = (J_\phi v_T)^\top(\cdot) = 0$), so $f \ne 0$ wherever
$v_T \ne 0$: no singular points where $\nabla\phi \neq 0$.

**Theorem 1.** $\dot\phi = J_\phi J_\phi^\top (J_\phi J_\phi^\top)^{-1} u_\phi = u_\phi$ wherever $J_\phi$ has full
rank. With $u_\phi = -k\phi$ the error decays as $\phi(t) = \phi(0)e^{-kt}$, whatever the path and its normalisation.

On the circle, $v_C = -k\,\phi\,\frac{r^2}{2\rho^2}\,d$, a radial velocity of $-k(\rho^2 - r^2)/(2\rho)$ m/s. It does
not depend on how $\phi$ is normalised: multiply $\phi$ by any constant and $v_C$ is the same.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# the classic field and the IK-GVF on the circle at three sizes, single integrators (this page's comparison)
cmp = []
for rr in [25.0, 100.0, 400.0]:
    P = path("circle", r=rr)
    p0 = [1.6 * rr, 0.0]
    row = [rr]
    for fld, kk in [("ik", 0.25), ("classic", 2500.0)]:
        run = run_si(P, p0, fld, kk, 10.0, 1.0, 0.01, 6000, every=10)
        ph = np.abs(np.array([q[3] for q in run])); tt = np.array([q[0] for q in run])
        a, b = np.argmax(ph < 0.3 * ph[0]), np.argmax(ph < 0.03 * ph[0])
        row.append(math.log(ph[a] / ph[b]) / (tt[b] - tt[a]) if b > a else float("nan"))
    cmp.append(row)
```

**What this page adds: the size of the path.** Single integrators, both fields with the same tangential speed of
10 m/s, from $1.6\,r$, the classic gain set once to $k = 2500$ (a good value for $r = 100$ m), the IK gain
$k = 0.25$. The measured decay rates of $|\phi|$:

```{python}

for rr, a, b in cmp:
```

The IK-GVF decays at its $k$ at every size; the classic field's rate follows $k\|\nabla\phi\|^2 \propto 1/r^2$. (An
aircraft flying the classic field normalised to its speed $v$ sees the rate $v k\|\nabla\phi\|$ near the path, so
$\propto 1/r$: the playground's approach race.) Try other paths and starts below.

## In three dimensions {#sec-m3}

```{python}
#| echo: false
r3 = run3("saddle", 50.0, 20.0, [75.0, -30.0, 35.0], [0.3, 0.8], 8.0, 0.001, 30000, every=50)
A3 = np.array(r3)
def fit_rate(t, y, lo=1e-4):
    m = (np.abs(y) > lo) & (t > 0.5)
    return -np.polyfit(t[m], np.log(np.abs(y[m])), 1)[0]
k1m, k2m = fit_rate(A3[:, 0], A3[:, 4]), fit_rate(A3[:, 0], A3[:, 5])
```

The paper states Theorem 1 for any dimension $m$. **What this page adds: one example with $m = 3$.** A closed path
shaped like the rim of a saddle is the intersection of two surfaces, the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ and the saddle
$z = h(x^2 - y^2)/r^2$, with $r = 50$ m and $h = 20$ m:

$$
\phi_1 = \frac{x^2 + y^2}{r^2} - 1, \qquad \phi_2 = \frac{1}{r}\left(z - h\,\frac{x^2 - y^2}{r^2}\right).
$$

$J_\phi$ is now $2 \times 3$. The tangent $v_T$ is along $\nabla\phi_1 \times \nabla\phi_2$, and
$v_C = J_\phi^\top (J_\phi J_\phi^\top)^{-1}u_\phi$ with $u_\phi = (-k_1\phi_1, -k_2\phi_2)$. Each error then
decays at its own rate. With $k_1 = 0.3$ and $k_2 = 0.8$ the simulation measures `{python} f3(k1m)` and
`{python} f3(k2m)`. The robot first reaches the saddle surface, then slides along it to the cylinder. The playground
has this example, and a path where Assumption 2 fails.

# Step 3: a behaviour around the path

The paper's Section III-B adds a time signal $\gamma(t)$ and a third part $v_B$, chosen so that

$$
J_\phi\,(v_C + v_B) = \dot\gamma - k\,(\phi - \gamma) \qquad \text{(the paper's (9))} .
$$

Then $\frac{d}{dt}(\phi - \gamma) = -k(\phi - \gamma)$: the error converges to $\gamma$, exponentially, at the rate
$k$. With $v_C = -\beta k\phi$ the paper's choice is $v_B = \beta(\dot\gamma + k\gamma)$, with
$\beta = J_\phi^\top(J_\phi J_\phi^\top)^{-1} = \nabla\phi/\|\nabla\phi\|^2$. Both terms of $v_B$ are needed. The
term $\beta\dot\gamma$ alone gives $\dot\phi = -k\phi + \dot\gamma$, whose steady state is $\gamma$ filtered by
$s/(s + k)$: smaller, and ahead in phase.

```{python}
#| echo: false
A2, w2 = WIGGLE2["A"], WIGGLE2["w"]
amp_only = A2 * w2 / math.hypot(w2, 0.25)
lead_only = math.degrees(math.atan2(0.25, w2))
```

For the paper's second flight, $\gamma(t) = A\sin(wt)$ with $A = 0.1$ and $w = 0.55$ rad/s (an 11.4 s period). On the
circle that is a radial swing of `{python} f2(circle_radial_error(A2, R))` m outwards and
`{python} f2(-circle_radial_error(-A2, R))` m inwards. Feeding forward only $\dot\gamma$ would give an amplitude of
`{python} f3(amp_only)` and a lead of `{python} f1(lead_only)`°.

# Step 4: an aircraft that cannot slow down

## The field at constant speed

The aircraft flies at the speed $v$ whatever it does, so the field it follows must have the length $v$. The paper's
template (11) keeps $\vartheta = v_C + v_B$, which sets $\dot\phi$, and fills the rest with the tangent:

$$
f = \alpha\,\hat v_T + \vartheta, \qquad \hat v_T = \frac{v_T}{\|v_T\|}, \qquad
\alpha = \sqrt{v^2 - \|\vartheta\|^2} .
$$

Because $\hat v_T \perp \vartheta$ (Lemma 1), $\|f\| = v$. This works only where $\|\vartheta\| \le v$, the set
$\Omega_b$. Outside it the paper flies straight along $\vartheta$ (its (12)):

$$
f = \begin{cases} v\,\vartheta/\|\vartheta\|, & \|\vartheta\| > v, \\ \alpha\,\hat v_T + \vartheta, & \|\vartheta\| \le v . \end{cases}
$$

The two pieces agree on the boundary, where $\alpha = 0$, so $f$ is continuous. Its units are metres per second
(Remark 3): $\vartheta$ is the velocity that sets the error, and $\alpha$ the speed left for travelling along the
path.

**$\Omega_b$ on the paper's circle.** Without $\gamma$, $\|\vartheta\| = k|\rho^2 - r^2|/(2\rho)$, so $\Omega_b$ is
the annulus $\rho^2 - r^2 \le 2v\rho/k$ on both sides. For $v = 15$ m/s and $k = 0.25$ it runs from
$\rho$ = `{python} f1(rin)` m to `{python} f1(rout)` m. Inside it, and with the heading aligned with $f$, the error
obeys $\dot\phi = -k\phi$ exactly (Theorem 1). Outside it the aircraft flies straight towards the path, along
$\nabla\phi$, and enters $\Omega_b$ in finite time. With a $\gamma$, $\vartheta$ changes with time and so does
$\Omega_b$; with wind, $v$ changes with the heading and so does $\Omega_b$.

```{=html}
<div id="ex-field" class="column-body"></div><script>EX.figs.wField("ex-field")</script>
```

# Step 5: the heading law

The aircraft must turn so that its velocity $\dot p$ lines up with $f$. Both have the length $v$. Theorem 2 commands

$$
\omega = \dot\theta_c + k_\theta\,\frac{f^\top E\,\dot p}{v^2}, \qquad \dot\theta_c = \frac{f^\top E^\top \dot f}{v^2} .
$$

$\dot\theta_c$ is the rate at which $f$ turns as seen by the moving aircraft (feed-forward), and
$f^\top E\dot p/v^2$ is the sine of the angle from $\dot p$ to $f$ (feedback). With $\varphi = \dot p - f$ and
$V = \|\varphi\|^2/2$, the paper finds $\dot V = -k_\theta(f^\top E\dot p)^2/v^2 \le 0$. The aircraft aligns unless it
starts flying exactly against the field, and Theorem 1 then holds along the flight.

**The derivative of $f$.** The law needs $\dot f$ along the motion. This page computes it exactly (the paper's
expressions after Theorem 2 differ, @sec-checks). With $\beta = \nabla\phi/\|\nabla\phi\|^2$,
$w = \dot\gamma - k(\phi - \gamma)$ and $\vartheta = \beta w$:

$$
\dot\beta = \frac{H_\phi\dot p}{\|\nabla\phi\|^2} - \frac{2\,\nabla\phi\,(\nabla\phi^\top H_\phi \dot p)}{\|\nabla\phi\|^4}, \qquad
\dot w = \ddot\gamma - k\,(\nabla\phi^\top\dot p - \dot\gamma), \qquad
\dot\vartheta = \dot\beta\,w + \beta\,\dot w ,
$$

and, writing $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{x}{\|x\|} = \frac{1}{\|x\|}\left(I - \frac{x x^\top}{\|x\|^2}\right)\dot x$,

$$
\dot f = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{v}{\|\vartheta\|}\left(I - \hat\vartheta\hat\vartheta^\top\right)\dot\vartheta, & \|\vartheta\| > v, \\[2mm]
\dot\alpha\,\hat v_T + \dfrac{\alpha}{\|v_T\|}\left(I - \hat v_T\hat v_T^\top\right)\dot v_T + \dot\vartheta, \quad \dot\alpha = -\dfrac{\vartheta^\top\dot\vartheta}{\alpha}, & \|\vartheta\| \le v ,
\end{cases}
$$

with $\dot v_T = s\,E H_\phi \dot p$. Note $\dot\alpha$: it divides by $\alpha$, which is zero on the boundary of
$\Omega_b$. @sec-checks measures what that does.

The figure below is the whole system, from any start, with the paper's gains of the first flight ($k = 0.25$,
$k_\theta = 0.6$) and its logged start: 323 m from the centre, heading 149°. The aircraft flies clockwise ($s = -1$),
as in the flights.

```{python}
# 3. the sign of gamma and the phase in flight 2
L2 = read_log("flight2")
g2 = L2["err"] - L2["phi"]                       # the logged error is phi + gamma (the repository's convention)
def sine_fit(t, y, w):
    M = np.c_[np.sin(w * t), np.cos(w * t), np.ones_like(t)]
    a, b, c = np.linalg.lstsq(M, y, rcond=None)[0]
    return math.hypot(a, b), math.atan2(b, a), c
ag, pg, _ = sine_fit(L2["t"], g2, 0.55)
```

The checks of this page, run against arXiv v1, found five things. None of them changes the paper's main results
(Lemma 1, Theorem 1, the flights). @sec-errata sums up where this page departs from arXiv v1 because of them.

**1. The heading rate is unbounded at the edge of $\Omega_b$.** The paper's Remark 2 asks for a field smooth enough
that the heading rate needed to track it is bounded. Field (12) is continuous, but $\alpha = \sqrt{v^2 - \|\vartheta\|^2}$
has an infinite slope where $\|\vartheta\| = v$, and $\dot\alpha = -\vartheta^\top\dot\vartheta/\alpha$ appears in
$\dot\theta_c$. An aircraft that enters $\Omega_b$ along $\vartheta$ sees $\alpha$ grow like $\sqrt\tau$, $\tau$ the time
since it entered, so $\dot\theta_c$ grows like $1/\sqrt\tau$. Flight 1 again, with a time step of 0.5 ms (it enters
at $t_b$ = `{python} f2(tb1)` s):

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| time after entering $\\Omega_b$ | $\\dot\\theta_c$ (rad/s) | $\\dot\\theta_c\\sqrt{\\tau}$ |\n|---|---|---|")
for tau, th, c in spike:
    print(f"| {tau:g} s | {th:.3f} | {c:.3f} |")
```

The product $\dot\theta_c\sqrt\tau$ stays between about 0.15 and 0.25 while $\dot\theta_c$ changes twentyfold: an
integrable singularity of the type $1/\sqrt\tau$. The field turns by a finite
angle, `{python} f0(turn1)`° in the first second, but no aircraft can follow its first instants. In the log of
flight 1 the commanded $\omega$ jumps from about 0 to `{python} f2(L1["omega"][il])` rad/s at the first sample inside
$\Omega_b$ (the spike of the paper's Fig. 3), and in the next five seconds the bank angle reaches
`{python} f0(np.abs(L1["bank"][il:il + 20]).max())`°, against about `{python} f0(np.abs(L1["bank"][L1["t"] > 40]).mean())`° on the circle. A $C^1$
blend between the two pieces of (12) would remove the spike; that is a design change, not a typo.

**2. The expressions for $\dot f$ after Theorem 2.** Taken literally, they differ from the exact derivative in two
places. (a) The text says that, outside $\Omega_b$, the term $v\left(\frac{I}{\|\vartheta\|} - \frac{\vartheta\vartheta^\top}{\|\vartheta\|^3}\right)\dot\vartheta$
vanishes because $\dot\vartheta$ is parallel to $\vartheta$. That holds only while $\nabla\phi$ keeps its direction,
for example on a circle flown exactly along the radius. In general $\nabla\phi$ turns as the aircraft moves, and so
does $\vartheta$. (b) $\dot\beta$ mixes $\dot p$ and $f$, which agree only once the aircraft is aligned. The turn rate of
the field, $\dot\theta_c$, at a few states (gains of flight 2, $\gamma$ of flight 2 at $t = 1$ s):

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| path and state | in $\\Omega_b$ | $\\dot\\theta_c$, exact | $\\dot\\theta_c$, as printed |\n|---|---|---|---|")
for nm, ins, a, b in tab_fd:
    print(f"| {nm} | {'yes' if ins else 'no'} | {a + 0.0:.4f} | {b + 0.0:.4f} |")
```

Outside $\Omega_b$ the printed expressions give a field that does not turn at all. The feedback term of the law
absorbs the difference: the aircraft is a little less aligned during the approach (about 1° more heading error),
and once in $\Omega_b$ the two versions fly the same. The largest $|\phi - \gamma|$ after 40 s, flying the second
flight's $\gamma$ from the start of flight 1, on four paths **[numerical]**:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| path | $\\dot f$ exact | $\\dot f$ as printed |\n|---|---|---|")
for nm, a, b in tab_fly:
    print(f"| {nm} | {a:.4f} | {b:.4f} |")
```

So the printed expressions cost nothing measurable in these flights, but they are not the derivative of $f$; this
page uses the exact ones (Step 5). The paper's code (the repository's `gvf_ik.py`)
writes its own derivatives, and its derivative of a unit vector has sign slips; this page does not reproduce it.

**3. The sign of $\gamma$, and the hand-adjusted phase of Fig. 4.** The paper drives $\phi \to \gamma$ (9). The code of
the paper's repository drives $e = \phi + \gamma$ to zero, so $\phi \to -\gamma$, and the flight log agrees: its
`GVF:error` column is $\phi + \gamma$, so the log holds the $\gamma$ that was flown. Fitting sines of
$w = 0.55$ rad/s to the 100 s of Fig. 4, $\phi$ and $-\gamma$ are in phase to `{python} f1(abs(lag2))`° (one log
sample is 8°). A design that feeds forward only $\dot\gamma$ would make $\phi$ *lead* by `{python} f0(lead_only)`°.
(The amplitudes differ: `{python} f3(ap)` for $\phi$ against `{python} f3(ag)` for $\gamma$. @sec-flights comes back to
it.) So the flight used the full $v_B$, as the caption of Fig. 4 in arXiv v1 also writes
($\dot\phi_p = \dot\gamma - k_\phi(\phi - \gamma)$), and its hand adjustment ("since we are inducing $\dot\gamma$
and not $\gamma$") is the clock offset and the sign: the hand-adjusted reference of the
figure and the logged $-\gamma$ have a correlation of `{python} f3(corr_hand)`.

**4. Two small slips.** The Jacobian of the circle in Section V misses a factor 2 in its second entry (@sec-phi). The
same section says that the error decreases "with time constant $k_\phi$"; $k_\phi$ is the rate, and the time constant
is $1/k_\phi$ = `{python} f0(1 / 0.25)` s.

**5. A dimension.** Section III-B defines $\gamma : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$; it is $\mathbb{R}^{m-1}$.

## Corrections at a glance {#sec-errata}

arXiv:2502.17313 v1 is the ICRA version. Where it is not correct, this page uses the correct version:

| where in arXiv v1 | arXiv v1 | this page |
|---|---|---|
| Theorem 2 and Remark 2 | $f$ and $\dot f$ sufficiently smooth in $\Omega_c$, heading rate bounded | $\dot f$ is unbounded on the edge of $\Omega_b$ (like $1/\sqrt\tau$, integrable): the spike of Fig. 3 (item 1) |
| after Theorem 2 | the term of $\dot f$ outside $\Omega_b$ "$= 0$" | it vanishes only when $\nabla\phi$ keeps its direction (item 2) |
| after Theorem 2 | $\dot\beta$ with $f$ in its last term | $\dot\beta = (I - 2\beta J_\phi) H_\phi \dot p / (J_\phi J_\phi^\top)$ (item 2, Step 5) |
| Fig. 4, caption | phase "adjusted by hand since we are inducing $\dot\gamma$ and not $\gamma$" | the flight used the full $v_B$, with $\phi \to -\gamma$; the adjustment is that sign and a clock offset (item 3) |
| Section V-A | $J_\phi = \frac{1}{r^2}[\,2(p_x - x_0)\ \ (p_y - y_0)\,]$ | $\frac{1}{r^2}[\,2(p_x - x_0)\ \ 2(p_y - y_0)\,]$ (item 4) |
| Section V-A | "with time constant $k_\phi$" | rate $k_\phi$, time constant $1/k_\phi$ (item 4) |
| Section III-B | $\gamma : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ | $\mathbb{R}^{m-1}$ (item 5) |

# The program the aircraft runs

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Before take-off, the aircraft knows:** the path, as $\phi$, $\nabla\phi$ and $H_\phi$ (here the circle: its centre
and radius); the direction $s$; the gains $k$ and $k_\theta$; the behaviour $\gamma(t)$, $\dot\gamma(t)$,
$\ddot\gamma(t)$.

**At every tick:** read the GPS position $p$, the course $\theta$ and the ground speed $v$; compute $\phi$,
$\nabla\phi$, $H_\phi$; compute $\vartheta$ and decide whether it is in $\Omega_b$; compute $f$ (12) and $\dot f$;
command $\omega = \dot\theta_c + k_\theta f^\top E\dot p/v^2$ to the autopilot. The onboard software uses the measured
ground speed as $v$, as the paper says, so the field always has the length the aircraft actually flies.
:::

In Python, for the paper's circle, the whole program is one function. The simulator runs the general version
(`ik_command` in the core below), and on the circle the two agree:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def program(p, theta, v, t, c, r, s, k, kth, A, w):
    """The aircraft, at every tick: position p, course theta, ground speed v, time t -> turn rate omega."""
    dx, dy = p[0] - c[0], p[1] - c[1]
    phi = (dx * dx + dy * dy) / r**2 - 1                         # the error signal
    g = [2 * dx / r**2, 2 * dy / r**2]                           # its gradient; the Hessian is (2/r^2) I
    gam, gamd, gamdd = A * math.sin(w * t), A * w * math.cos(w * t), -A * w * w * math.sin(w * t)
    pd = [v * math.cos(theta), v * math.sin(theta)]
    n2 = g[0] ** 2 + g[1] ** 2
    W = gamd - k * (phi - gam)                                   # the rate the error must have
    th = [g[0] * W / n2, g[1] * W / n2]                          # vartheta = v_C + v_B
    thn = math.hypot(*th)
    Hp = [2 * pd[0] / r**2, 2 * pd[1] / r**2]
    gHp = g[0] * Hp[0] + g[1] * Hp[1]
    Wd = gamdd - k * (g[0] * pd[0] + g[1] * pd[1] - gamd)
    thd = [(Hp[i] - 2 * g[i] * gHp / n2) / n2 * W + g[i] * Wd / n2 for i in range(2)]
    if thn > v:                                                  # outside Omega_b: straight along vartheta
        f = [v * th[0] / thn, v * th[1] / thn]
        q = (th[0] * thd[0] + th[1] * thd[1]) / thn**2
        fd = [v * (thd[i] - th[i] * q) / thn for i in range(2)]
    else:                                                        # inside: the tangent fills the speed
        n = math.sqrt(n2)
        T = [-s * g[1] / n, s * g[0] / n]
        Td0 = [-s * Hp[1], s * Hp[0]]
        q = T[0] * Td0[0] + T[1] * Td0[1]
        Td = [(Td0[i] - T[i] * q) / n for i in range(2)]
        al = math.sqrt(v * v - thn * thn)
        ald = -(th[0] * thd[0] + th[1] * thd[1]) / al if al > 1e-12 else 0.0
        f = [al * T[i] + th[i] for i in range(2)]
        fd = [ald * T[i] + al * Td[i] + thd[i] for i in range(2)]
    thc = (f[0] * fd[1] - f[1] * fd[0]) / v**2                  # the turn rate of the field
    return thc + kth * (f[1] * pd[0] - f[0] * pd[1]) / v**2     # + k_theta f^T E p' / v^2
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
gap = 0.0
for _ in range(200):
    st = {"x": float(rng.uniform(-300, 300)), "y": float(rng.uniform(-300, 300)), "psi": float(rng.uniform(-3, 3))}
    t = float(rng.uniform(0, 50)); v = float(rng.uniform(12, 18))
    a = program([st["x"], st["y"]], st["psi"], v, t, [0, 0], 100.0, -1.0, 0.25, 0.8, 0.1, 0.55)
    b = ik_command(CIRCLE, st, v, FLIGHT2, gamma(WIGGLE2, t))["omega"]
    gap = max(gap, abs(a - b))
```

On 200 random states, `program` and the simulator's `ik_command` differ by at most `{python} e1(gap)` rad/s.

# The simulator

The world, not the aircraft: the position and the course are integrated with Euler ticks of 10 ms, with $\omega$
held during a tick. The wind adds to the airspeed, so the ground speed changes with the course; the program measures
it, as the onboard software does. The box below holds the complete core of this page (click to open it).

# Running it: the paper's flights again {#sec-flights}

The paper's repository keeps the telemetry logs of the flights. This page reads them (the windows that drew the
paper's figures, `data/README.md`) and runs the same flights in the simulator: airspeed 15 m/s, a wind of 2 m/s
(the paper says "around 2 m/s"; the direction is chosen to match the logged 17 m/s at the start of flight 1), and
the paper's gains. The logs arrive at 4 Hz, and positions at about 1 Hz.

## Flight 1: the designed transient (the paper's Fig. 3)

```{python}
#| echo: false
S1 = np.array(fly(CIRCLE, START1, FLIGHT1, VA, WIND, DT, 10000, every=5))
ibs = int(np.argmax(S1[:, 10] > 0)); tbs = S1[ibs, 0]
def decay(t, ph, t0, t1):
    m = (t >= t0) & (t <= t1) & (np.abs(ph) > 0.02)
    return -np.polyfit(t[m], np.log(np.abs(ph[m])), 1)[0]
rate_log = decay(L1["t"], L1["phi"], 8.0, 20.0)
rate_sim = decay(S1[:, 0], S1[:, 4], tbs, tbs + 12)
phi0_log = L1["phi"][0]
mL = L1["t"] >= 8.0
pred_log = L1["phi"][L1["t"] < 8.0][-1] * np.exp(-0.25 * (L1["t"][mL] - 8.0))
dev_log = float(np.abs(L1["phi"][mL] - pred_log).max())
mS = S1[:, 0] >= tbs
dev_sim = float(np.abs(S1[mS, 4] - S1[ibs, 4] * np.exp(-0.25 * (S1[mS, 0] - tbs))).max())
```

The aircraft starts at $\phi$ = `{python} f2(phi0_log)`, about 323 m from the centre. Outside $\Omega_b$ it flies
straight in; the log shows $\|v_T\| = \alpha = 0$ there, as (12) says. The log enters $\Omega_b$ at
`{python} f2(L1["t"][il])` s (the paper marks 8 s), the simulation at `{python} f2(tbs)` s. Then $\phi$ decays. Fitted
over the next 12 s, the log decays at `{python} f3(rate_log)` and the simulation at `{python} f3(rate_sim)`, for a
designed $k = 0.25$. The largest gap between the log and the paper's prediction $\phi_p$ (from 8 s) is
`{python} f2(dev_log)`, in the simulation `{python} f3(dev_sim)`: the wind, the 1 Hz positions and the aircraft's own
roll dynamics are not in the model.

